# Codex — plugin enablement, hook trust and the subagents copy (read by `/b6p-setup` step 1)

Applies when `/b6p-setup` runs inside Codex.


If `/b6p-setup` is running in Codex, the marketplace and the plugin are already installed. (For a teammate who has not installed yet: `codex plugin marketplace add Bluestep-Systems/bluestep-ai` — CLI, or the same repo from the plugins screen in the desktop app — then install `bluestep-tools` from it.)

**Marketplace registration (read only).** Read the `source` of `[marketplaces.bluestep]` in `~/.codex/config.toml` (`$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` when `CODEX_HOME` is set). Never write the file. The entry names the old repo if its `source` is a URL naming `github.com/Bluestep-Systems/bspecs` (with or without `.git`, any case) or is `Bluestep-Systems/bspecs`. If it names the old repo, put one note under the report's notes, never under what the machine still lacks: nothing is needed, updates follow the repo's rename. To move anyway, run `codex plugin marketplace remove bluestep`, then `codex plugin marketplace add Bluestep-Systems/bluestep-ai` — the plugins stay installed and their hooks stay trusted.

What remains are two steps that are easy to miss and that the tooling genuinely depends on:

- **Trust the hooks — they silently do nothing until you do.** Open the plugin's page and use **Review → trust** on its hooks (`/hooks` in the CLI). An untrusted hook produces no error and no log; the guardrails simply never run. **Re-trust is required after any release that changes a hook definition**, so re-check this after a plugin update. Check `ls ~/.codex/agents/` while you are here (next bullet).
- **Subagents do not come from the plugin on Codex.** A plugin cannot register them there, so the three BlueStep subagents have to be copied by hand into `~/.codex/agents/` — once per machine, covers every project. (A project's own `.codex/agents/` also works, but then it is a per-project step.) The three files are `b6p_task_implementer.toml`, `b6p_commenter.toml` and `b6p_code_review.toml` (TOML, underscore names — hyphens are not valid agent names on Codex). They sit in the installed plugin's `agents/` folder, next to its `skills/` folder, and in the bluestep-ai repo at `dist/codex/bluestep-tools/agents/` (`https://github.com/Bluestep-Systems/bluestep-ai/tree/main/dist/codex/bluestep-tools/agents`). If you can find the installed plugin's `agents/` folder, give the user the exact `cp` command for the three files into `~/.codex/agents/` — hand it over, do not run it (`~/.codex/` is outside the project); otherwise give them the three filenames and the repo path. Until the copy is done, say plainly that delegation is unavailable on Codex and the spec skills run in-session instead of handing work to a subagent. Do not pretend a subagent exists.

**phi-guard (opt-in).** A separate plugin in the same marketplace, listed next to `bluestep-tools`: it blocks an agent's write that looks like real client data. Codex runs it through a generated wrapper, which may not see every write. It is installed per machine, acts only in a B6P project (a `U######/` folder or the `AGENTS.md` marker `/b6p-setup` writes), and stays silent everywhere else. Ask the user whether `phi-guard` shows as installed on Codex's plugins screen, folded into the offer. Missing → offer it, and on a yes hand over the steps: on Codex, install `phi-guard` from the marketplace, then **trust its hook** the same way as above (Review → trust, `/hooks` in the CLI) — until then it does nothing, and it needs re-trust after a release that changes it. To turn it off for one project on Codex, a `*` line in that project's `.phi-allow` does it, but it also turns off the git client-data check. That git check, which `/b6p-setup` sets up in step 2, runs with or without the plugin.

The gateway MCP server ships with the plugin and comes up once `B6PT_TOKEN` is set (`references/platform-token.md`) — note that GUI apps only see the environment they were launched with, so a token set in a shell session does not reach them.
